vignette:
He is a 40-year-old Middle Eastern man who has worked as a paramedic for many years, and for most of that time he has thought of himself as steady in a crisis. His wife describes him as the kind of person who is calm when everyone else is panicking, the one who knows what to do and does it without hesitation. He has built his life around being useful, reliable, and hard to shake. That image changed after the night his younger brother was seriously injured in a traffic collision.

He is still able to tell the story in careful, practical detail, as if he is reporting a call. He remembers the phone ringing late, the clipped voice on the other end, the location, the sick feeling before the words were even clear. When he arrived at the scene, he saw the wrecked car before he saw his brother. The road was lit by emergency lights and headlights, the air heavy with fuel, glass, and shouting. He moved automatically at first, reaching for the skills that usually keep fear at a distance. Then he recognized his brother’s watch, then his face, and the world narrowed. He describes feeling as though his body kept working while his mind went briefly elsewhere, as if he were watching another man kneel in the road and call his brother’s name.

His brother survived, but the injuries were severe and the recovery long. In the weeks that followed, he was torn between his role as a medic and his role as family. At work, he continued answering emergency calls, but something in him had changed. He notices that he scans every crushed vehicle for a familiar shape, every hospital corridor for news he does not want to hear. He starts arriving at scenes with his jaw already clenched. He is more irritated with coworkers, more impatient with small talk, more likely to snap and then feel ashamed. He tells himself he needs to stay functional for his wife and children, but at home he is often distant, sitting in the dark after his shifts with the television on and no real attention on it.

Sleep becomes difficult. He falls asleep exhausted and wakes suddenly, heart racing, with the sense that something terrible has just happened. Some nights he dreams of the crash, not as it was but with small changes that make it worse: his brother calling out, his hands not moving fast enough, the road stretching farther away. He avoids driving certain routes. He stops volunteering for calls that involve serious motor vehicle accidents when he can, though he dislikes admitting this to himself. He also avoids visiting the section of the hospital where his brother first stayed because the smell of antiseptic and the sound of monitors bring the whole night back into his body.

What troubles him most is how easily the memory intrudes. A siren in traffic, the sound of metal scraping, even the sight of a brother and sister walking together in a parking lot can suddenly pull him back to that road. In those moments his chest tightens, his mouth goes dry, and he feels briefly as though he is there again, unable to move past the image of the wreck. He becomes angry at himself for not being stronger. He has spent years helping strangers through their worst moments, and he is ashamed that this one event has shaken him so deeply. At times he wonders whether he failed his brother, though he knows logically that he could not have prevented the crash.

In sessions, he speaks with restraint, often pausing as if checking whether he is allowed to say more. He does not present as a man who easily asks for help. Yet beneath his controlled manner there is grief that has nowhere to go, and a constant alertness that has made ordinary life feel thinner and less safe. He loves his wife and children, but he finds himself less present with them than he wants to be, as though part of him remains on that road waiting for the outcome to change. He continues to work, continue to function, continue to show up, but he does so with an effort that leaves him drained and watchful, carrying the memory of his brother’s accident into nearly every part of his day.
